docs.title: Boundary recommendation
docs.text: Keep control, planning, and safety interfaces narrow and message-based. This reduces coupling between simulator, hardware, and higher-level behaviors.

docs.title: Branching
docs.text:
• Create feature branches from development
  • Keep pull requests focused and small when possible

docs.title: Before opening a pull request
docs.text:
Run all automated checks:

pre-commit run --all-files

docs.title: Commit style
docs.text:
Use clear commit messages with a scope prefix, for example:

  • hardware: improve motor timeout handling
  • sim: add mujoco contact debug view
  • docs: update control loop diagram

docs.title: Team conventions
docs.text:
• Prefer message/interface changes in humanoid_interfaces before cross-package rewrites
  • Document any new topic/service/action in docs
  • Add tests for all non-trivial behavior changes

docs.title: Python API Standards (Team Checklist)
docs.text: Use this checklist when writing or modifying Python code so API docs remain useful and python -m mkdocs build --strict stays green.

docs.title: 1) Add type annotations for all public APIs
docs.text:
Include type hints for:

  • Function/method parameters
  • Return values
  • Public dataclass fields / attributes where practical

Example:

def compute_torque(q: np.ndarray, dq: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    ...

docs.title: 2) Write docstrings for public modules, classes, and functions
docs.text:
Use triple-quoted docstrings and describe:

  • Purpose
  • Key arguments
  • Return value
  • Units and coordinate frames for robotics quantities

Example:

def step(self, dt: float) -> None:
    """Advance simulation by one time step.

    Args:
        dt: Step size in seconds.
    """

docs.title: 3) Keep signatures stable and explicit
docs.text:
• Avoid overly-generic *args/**kwargs for public APIs unless necessary.
  • If needed, explain forwarded arguments in docstrings.

docs.title: 4) Document shapes and conventions
docs.text:
For vectors/matrices, include shape and meaning in docstrings:

  • q: (n_joints,) joint positions [rad]
  • J: (6, n_joints) geometric Jacobian

docs.title: 5) Avoid undocumented magic values
docs.text:
• Replace literals with named constants.
  • Explain thresholds/tolerances in docstrings or comments.

docs.title: 6) Keep imports and formatting clean
docs.text:
Before commit, run:

pre-commit run --all-files

This runs Ruff, mypy, clang-format, and docs validation hooks.

docs.title: 7) Add a minimal usage example for new core APIs
docs.text:
For important new classes/functions, add a short example in:

  • docs/api/python/ (one page per module) for API visibility, or
  • package README/docs page for workflow context.

docs.title: 8) Treat docs build as a required quality gate
docs.text:
Always ensure this passes locally before PR:

python -m mkdocs build --strict

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
The Python API reference is split by module, one page per module. All Python packages under src/ are documented:

  • humanoid_pinocchio – rigid-body model (FK, IK, Jacobians, dynamics, centroidal)
  • humanoid_utils – rotations, Kalman filter family, time utilities
  • mujoco_sim – MuJoCo simulator node
  • humanoid_monitor – standalone monitoring GUI (ROS/Qt bridge, theme, plots, state-estimation views)
  • humanoid_state_estimator – EKF state estimator (state, process/measurement models, initialization, evaluation, node interface)
  • humanoid_contact_detection – foot-contact ground truth and leg-odometry nodes

Packages without a Python API (humanoid_interfaces IDL, humanoid_description assets, humanoid_bringup launch, humanoid_hardware/humanoid_safety/humanoid_tests C++) are covered by the C++ API instead.

Each page documents the module's public API as auto-generated by mkdocstrings.

Displays one estimator bias at a time: - Gyroscope bias - Accelerometer bias

docs.title: MonitorNode
docs.text:
MonitorNode(bridge)

Bases: Node

ROS subscriber node for humanoid_monitor.

docs.title: humanoid_state_estimator.process_models.dynamics
docs.text:
Continuous and discrete dynamics model

State:

x = [ q_BW, p_W, v_W, b_g_B, b_a_B, a_B ]

  • a_B is the true coordinate acceleration expressed in the body frame, with first-order Gauss-Markov dynamics in body frame:

    a_dot_B = -a_B / tau_acc

Input:

u = omega_m_B

Measured angular velocity expressed in Body frame.

Rotation convention (INav3):

quaternion_to_rotation_matrix(q) returns the rotation tensor R (Eq. 348). For q_BW this is R_BW, mapping body-frame vector components to world-frame components (x_W = R_BW @ x_B). Velocity dynamics is therefore v_dot_W = R_BW @ a_B. Its transpose is the transformation matrix T_BW = R_BW.T (Eq. 214), mapping world components to body components.

R and T are NOT the same; do not confuse them.

discrete_dynamics(x, u, dt, tau_acc=None)

Discrete state transition.

x(k+1)=f_d(x(k),u(k))

quaternion_bias_jacobian(q_BW)

Compute:

dq_dot / db_g_B

Model:

omega_B =
    omega_m_B - b_g_B


q_dot =
    1/2 q_BW ⊗ omega_B

continuous_dynamics_jacobian(x, u, tau_acc=None)

Conventions (INav3 attitude representation):

  • Subscript W denotes vectors expressed in the world frame.
  • Subscript B denotes vectors expressed in the body frame.
  • q_BW is the rotation quaternion of the body frame wrt the world frame. quaternion_to_rotation_matrix(q_BW) is the rotation tensor R_BW (Eq. 348):
    x_W = R_BW @ x_B

The transformation matrix T_BW = R_BW.T maps the other way:

    x_B = T_BW @ x_W        (Eq. 214)

R and T are transposes of each other; do not confuse them. - a_B is the true coordinate acceleration (p_ddot_W) expressed in the body frame: a_B = T_BW @ a_W.

docs.title: EKF
docs.text:
EKF(x0, P0, f, F, Q, L=None)

Bases: KF

Discrete-time Extended Kalman Filter.

The filter follows the nonlinear model

x_k = f(x_{k-1}, ...)
z_k = h(x_k, ...)

with covariance propagation based on the Jacobians F, L, H, and M.

Initialize the Extended Kalman Filter.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x0 Any

Initial state estimate.

required P0 Any

Initial estimation-error covariance.

required f Callable[..., Any]

Discrete nonlinear process model.

required F Model

State Jacobian of the process model.

required Q Any

Process-noise covariance.

required L Optional[Model]

Process-noise Jacobian/gain matrix. If None, additive process noise is assumed and L = I.

None

docs.title: predict
docs.text:
predict(*args, **kwargs)

Perform the EKF prediction step.

Computes

x^- = f(x^+, ...)
P^- = F P^+ F^T + L Q L^T

Additional positional and keyword arguments are forwarded to the process model and its Jacobians.

docs.title: update
docs.text:
update(z, h, H, R, M=None, residual=None, *args, **kwargs)

Perform the EKF measurement-update step.

Computes

innovation = z - h(x^-)
S = H P^- H^T + M R M^T
K = P^- H^T S^-1
x^+ = x^- + K innovation

The covariance is updated using the Joseph stabilized form.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default z Any

Measurement vector.

required h Callable[..., Any]

Nonlinear measurement model.

required H Model

Measurement-model state Jacobian.

required R Any

Measurement-noise covariance.

required M Optional[Model]

Measurement-noise Jacobian/gain matrix. If None, additive measurement noise is assumed and M = I.

None residual Optional[Callable[..., Any]]

Optional custom residual function. This is useful for quantities such as wrapped angles.

None

Additional positional and keyword arguments are forwarded to h, H, and M.

quaternion_to_rotation_matrix(q)

Quaternion to rotation tensor R.

x_W = R_BW @ x_B

The transformation matrix (world -> body) is its transpose (Eq. 214/350):

T_BW = R_BW.T,  x_B = T_BW @ x_W

Do not confuse the two: R != T.

docs.title: unwrap_angles
docs.text:
unwrap_angles(angles, period=TWO_PI)

Reconstruct the continuous series behind a wrapped angle sequence.

Each sample is replaced by the representative nearest to its predecessor, so a crossing of the wrap boundary continues smoothly: 179, -179 degrees becomes 179, 181 rather than jumping back.

The whole series is unwrapped at once, so the result stays continuous as a consumer inspects different time windows; unwrapping each visible window independently would make the curve move when the window moves.

Non-finite samples are handled by unwrapping each contiguous finite run separately, leaving the non-finite samples untouched. This matters because unwrapping is cumulative: without segmentation, one NaN would corrupt every later value.

After unwrapping, values drift outside the bounded range, growing by one full turn per revolution. That is the intended trade for continuity. Use :func:wrap_to_pi afterwards if the bounded range is needed.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
angles: 1D array of wrapped angle values.

period

Length of one full turn in the unit of angles.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: numpy.ndarray Continuous angle values, with the same length as the input.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: import numpy as np degrees = np.array([178.0, 179.0, -179.0, -178.0]) unwrap_angles(degrees, period=360.0) array([178., 179., 181., 182.])

docs.title: align_angles_to_reference
docs.text:
align_angles_to_reference(
    reference,
    values,
    reference_time=None,
    values_time=None,
    period=TWO_PI,
)

Shift an angle series onto a reference angle series.

Two series that are each internally continuous can still differ by a whole number of turns, because unwrapping is a per-series operation: an estimate that starts at 10 degrees and a ground truth that starts at -350 degrees describe the same rotation. Compared naively they look completely wrong.

This function removes that ambiguity by adding the nearest multiple of one full turn to values so it lands on reference.

The offset is the median of reference - values over the overlapping part of the session, rounded to a whole number of turns. The median makes it robust to individual outliers, and the rounding is what keeps the operation safe: only the arbitrary period * k ambiguity is removed, the genuine difference between the two series is never touched.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
reference: 1D reference series, typically the estimate.

values

1D series to be shifted onto the reference. Assumed to be continuous already, e.g. after :func:unwrap_angles.

reference_time

Optional 1D timestamps matching reference.

values_time

Optional 1D timestamps matching values. Both time arguments must be given together; when they are, values is interpolated onto the reference timestamps inside their overlapping span.

period

Length of one full turn in the unit of the series.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: numpy.ndarray values shifted by a whole number of turns, unchanged when there is not enough data to estimate an offset.
